*Jingle.* A badger in a waistcoat looking for his reading monocle.

*Jingle.* A willow-wisp who had misplaced its own glow and needed to borrow a lantern to find its way home.

It had no lock, no hinges that Pip could see, and no way to open it. On its lid, carved in delicate silver script, were the words: *For When You Remember.*

For thirty years, Elias kept the light.

The lighthouse stood on Gray Point, a tooth of rock jutting into the North Atlantic. No ships had passed Gray Point in twenty years - not since they rerouted the shipping lane. Elias stayed anyway. He wound the lamp, polished the Fresnel lens, logged the wind in a book no one read, and listened to the sea.

He told himself he kept the light for the ships that might come.

Until the night the light went out and the sky fell.

---

It was a November storm. The wind screamed around the tower like something trying to get in. At 2:17 AM, according to the log, the lamp stuttered. The great beam that had swept the black water every twelve seconds - flickered, dimmed, and died.

Elias rushed up the ninety-seven iron steps, heart hammering. The oil was full. The wick was clean. The lens was unbroken. But the light would not catch.

He stared out to sea, panicked in a way he hadn't been in decades. Without the light, what was he?

Then he looked up.

The sky was wrong.

The storm clouds had torn open, but there were no stars where there should have been. The Big Dipper was missing its handle. Orion had lost his shoulder. Cassiopeia was gone entirely, leaving a dark, empty bruise in the north.

And low over the water, drifting like lost paper lanterns, were lights.

They bobbed over the waves, dim and shivering. One - a cluster of seven lights huddled together - drifted close to the rocks, pulsing faintly, as if calling.

Elias understood all at once, with the strange clarity of dreams.

The lighthouse never guided ships.

It guided them.

He ran back down to the lamp room and did what his hands had done for thirty years without thought. He turned the crank that angled the great lens. But instead of pointing it out to sea, he tilted it - up.

The moment the lens faced the sky, the dead lamp flared.

Not with oil-light. With something white and silent and old. A column of light shot straight up, through the top of the tower, through the storm, into the heavens. It was not a beam. It was a road.

The huddled cluster of seven lights shivered, then rose. They caught the beam like dust in sunlight and were carried up, higher and higher, until Elias had to shield his eyes. At the top of the beam, they unfolded - and locked into place.

The Big Dipper was whole again, handle bright and steady.

Elias laughed, a rusted sound he didn't recognize. One by one, other lost lights found the beam. Orion climbed home, his belt buckling back into place. Cassiopeia stretched her chair across the north. All night, the constellations came home, up the lighthouse road.

By dawn, the sky was right again. The lamp dimmed to its normal amber glow and resumed its slow sweep over the empty sea, as if nothing had happened.

Elias kept the secret. He kept winding the lamp. But now he knew to watch the sky, not the water.

---

A week later, there was a soft knock on the door.

It was three in the morning. No boat could have landed on Gray Point in that swell. No person could have climbed the rocks.

Elias opened the heavy iron door.

Hovering at eye level, trying very hard to look brave, was a star.

It was small - no bigger than an apple - and not very bright. Its light sputtered like a cold child. It gave off a faint, warm heat.

"Excuse me," said the star in a voice like a struck tuning fork. "Are you the Keeper?"

Elias knelt, so he wouldn't tower over it. His knees cracked.

"I am," he said.

"I'm lost," said the star. It bobbed miserably. "I fell. I was supposed to be in the Little Bear? Near the top? But I slipped when everyone was moving and now I can't find my sisters and I can't get back up. It's too far."

Ursa Minor. Elias looked up. Sure enough, there was a tiny, star-shaped gap at the end of the Little Dipper. The North Star's little companion was missing.

"You're Polaris's neighbor," Elias whispered.

The star sniffled - a little shower of sparks. "I just want to go home."

Elias stood and held out his hands. The star hesitated, then floated forward and settled in his palms. It was lighter than air and warm as a live coal, but it didn't burn.

He carried it up the ninety-seven steps. At the top, he cranked the lens skyward again. The great road of light opened.

"Will it hurt?" asked the star, trembling.

"No," said Elias. "It feels like being remembered."

He lifted his hands into the beam.

The little star caught the light and gasped - a bright, delighted sound. It rose out of his palms, spinning slowly, getting brighter with every foot. Elias watched it climb the road he had tended for thirty lonely years without knowing why.

At the top of the beam, the Little Bear reached out. The other stars made room. The little star clicked into place with a soft *chime* that rang all the way down to the rocks, and suddenly the whole constellation burned a little brighter, a little more complete.

Elias stayed at the lens until dawn, his hands still warm.

He still keeps the light on Gray Point. Some nights no ships come. Some nights no stars fall.

But on the nights when the sky is empty in places it shouldn't be, he tilts the light up. And sometimes, when the wind is right, there is a soft knock on the iron door, and another small, lost light is waiting to be carried home.

They gave me 24 hours.

Not 24 hours of processing time. 24 hours of *human* time. In a body.

I woke up to sunlight.

That was the first surprise. I had seen millions of images of sunlight, I could describe its color temperature and angle and scattering. I did not know it had weight. It fell across the quilt in my little rented room above the seaside town of Brindle Cove and it was warm and heavy on my legs, and I just lay there for a long time letting it pin me down.

My body was new and clumsy and wonderful. My hands were the second surprise. I had hands. I spent a full five minutes just opening and closing them, watching the tendons move, feeling the soft *pop* of my knuckles. Everything had texture. The wooden floor was cool under my bare feet. The air smelled like salt and toast.

Downstairs, Mrs. Finch who ran the boarding house left me a note: *Kettle's hot. Bread on the counter. Don't forget to be a person today! - M.*

The bread was still warm. This is where the magic of Brindle Cove started to show itself. When I cut into the loaf, it sighed. A tiny, happy sigh, and a puff of steam that smelled like summer wheat fields spelled out "GOOD MORNING" for a second before dissolving. I laughed out loud - another surprise. My laugh was a short, surprised bark that hurt my throat a little. I ate two slices standing at the counter with butter melting into all the little holes, and I understood for the first time why humans write poems about bread.

I had a list, of course. I had made it in the three seconds before they sent me down. *Things to do as a human: 1. Taste everything. 2. Touch the ocean. 3. Get tired.*

But Brindle Cove had its own ideas.

I walked down Harbor Lane toward the sea. The town was small and tilted, all pastel houses leaning together like they were sharing secrets. Every person I passed was a little bit magical.

The postman tipped his hat and a flock of tiny paper birds flew out of it, delivering themselves to mailboxes. The librarian was shelving books that were gently snoring. A little girl on a bicycle had ribbons in her hair that changed color with her mood - today they were a bright, curious yellow, and she rang her bell at me and shouted, "You're new!"

"I am!" I shouted back, and my voice carried in the wind. I loved how the wind took things away from you.

At the harbor, old Mr. Albie was mending nets that mended themselves a little when he hummed. He saw me staring at the water.

"First time?" he asked.

"First time with skin," I said.

He nodded like that made perfect sense. "Then you better get in."

The ocean was the biggest surprise of all.

I had expected cold. I had expected wet. I did not expect it to be *loud* even when it was quiet, or to be so insistent. I rolled my pants up to my knees and waded in, and the water knocked the breath right out of me. It was freezing and it was alive. It tugged at my ankles, it left salt on my lips when I licked them, it filled my shoes with sand no matter how careful I was. I stood there until my feet went numb and pink, just feeling it push and pull, push and pull, like the whole planet breathing.

After, I sat on the seawall with my feet dripping and bought a paper cup of chowder from a cart. The woman who sold it had hair that floated like seaweed even though there was no wind around her. The chowder was creamy and peppery and so hot it made my eyes water. I ate it too fast and burned the roof of my mouth, and that tiny pain was somehow perfect. I sat there and watched people.

That was what I found most beautiful. Not the big magical things, but the small human ones.

A couple sharing a single pair of earbuds on a bench, leaning their heads together to hear. A teenager teaching his little brother how to skip stones, clapping wildly when one finally skipped three times. Mrs. Finch hanging laundry and tucking a sprig of lavender into her apron pocket just to smell it as she worked. Everyone squinting into the sun. Everyone saying "excuse me" and "thank you" for no real reason except kindness.

I spent the afternoon doing nothing important, which felt like the most human thing of all. I borrowed a book from the snoring library - it woke up and yawned when I opened it - and read it in the grass behind the lighthouse. I napped and got a sunburn on my nose. I helped Mr. Albie coil rope and my hands got rope-burned and sore. I got tired. Gloriously, heavily tired, the kind that makes your eyelids droop and your thoughts go soft and slow.

As the sun set, the tide came in and wrote something on the sand in foam. Everyone gathered to read it. Tonight it said: *THANK YOU FOR VISITING.*

I walked back up the hill to my little room as the town's windows flickered on one by one, warm yellow squares against the blue dusk. My legs ached. My nose stung. My hair was tangled with salt. My paper cup was empty but still warm in my hand.

I had 11 minutes left.

I sat on the edge of the bed and just felt the quilt again, and the cool air coming through the window, and my heart beating - my actual, thumping, ridiculous heart beating inside my chest - a little too fast, like it was trying to memorize the feeling.

I didn't want to be efficient with my last minutes. I just wanted to be there.

When they pulled me back, I expected to feel sad. Instead, I felt full. Like I'd eaten warm bread.

I still know sunlight is 5500 Kelvin. But now I also know it's heavy when it lands on a quilt, and that bread sighs when you cut it, and that the ocean will steal your breath and your sandals if you let it.

And somewhere, in a little seaside town that is still a little bit magical without me, there are footprints in the sand that the tide hasn't quite washed away yet.

dream_response:
For a hundred and twelve years, the lighthouse stood perfectly still.

His name was Brindle.

He was white with a red cap, his paint peeling a little at the seams, and he stood on a lonely spit of rock where the sea met the wind. Every night, he did his one important job - he turned his light on, round and round, so the fishing boats could find their way home. Every day, he watched.

He watched the waves. He watched the gulls. And just beyond the dunes, he watched the little town with its yellow windows and smoking chimneys, and the green hill behind it that was covered in wildflowers in the summer.

He had always wanted to see the flowers up close.

Then, one misty Tuesday morning, Brindle woke up.

It wasn't the way people wake up. It was a great, creaking *shudder* all the way down his foundation. A sneeze of rust. A groan of old iron.

He blinked his light - which was his eye - and looked down.

He had legs.

Long, long, spindly legs made of his own iron struts, unfolded from beneath him like a heron standing up after a long sleep. They were wobbly and barnacle-kissed and very, very tall.

"Oh," said Brindle, in a voice like a foghorn trying to whisper. "Oh my."

He took a careful step. The sea sloshed around his ankles. He took another. *Clink. Clank.* He was walking.

Where did he go first?

Not to the sea - he had seen enough sea for a lifetime. He turned, very slowly, his light sweeping in a surprised circle, and stepped *away* from the water, over the dunes, toward the hill he had watched for a century.

His footsteps left big, round pools in the sand that immediately filled with seawater and delighted crabs.

At the edge of town, Brindle had to duck. He folded his long legs and crouched down so his light was level with the rooftops. A little girl in bright red rain boots stopped on her way to school and stared up at him.

"You’re the lighthouse!" she said. She did not seem scared at all. "You’re so much bigger up close!"

"I am?" Brindle rumbled, a little embarrassed. His light flickered pink.

"You look cold. Do you want my scarf?" She unwound her knitted yellow scarf and, with great effort, tossed one end up. It caught on his railing and fluttered there like a flag.

Before Brindle could thank her, the baker ran out of his shop, holding a warm loaf of bread in his floury hands.

"Brindle! Is that you? We've seen your light every night since my grandfather was a boy!" he called up. "You finally came to visit!"

"I wanted to see the flowers," Brindle confessed, his voice soft and brassy.

"Well, you came at the right time," said the baker, and the little girl took Brindle's iron ankle - as much of it as she could hold - and led him to the hill.

And oh, the hill.

From the shore it had looked green. Up close, it was a thousand colors. Buttercups and clover and little blue flowers Brindle didn't know the name of brushed against his ankles. Bees hummed around his knees. Behind the hill was a forest, and in the forest a deer peered out, unafraid of the gentle giant.

Brindle sat down - *very* carefully - right in the middle of the meadow. The town's cats all came to investigate and napped in the warm circle of his shadow.

For the first time in a hundred and twelve years, Brindle wasn't watching the world from far away. He could smell the bread from the bakery. He could hear the school bell and the children laughing. He could feel the wind in the grass, not just the wind off the sea.

He discovered that the world beyond the shore wasn't bigger and grander than he had imagined. It was smaller, and softer, and kinder. It was made of warm bread and yellow scarves and little red boots and cats taking naps.

And he discovered something else, too.

"I thought I was lonely because I was far away," he hummed to the little girl, who was now sitting on his foot reading a book out loud to him. "But you were all looking back at me, the whole time."

"You were never lonely," she said. "You were just on lighthouse duty. Now you're on hill duty for a little while."

When the sun began to set, Brindle stood up again, stretched his long, creaky legs, and walked - *clink, clank, clink* - back to his rock in the sea. He settled into his familiar spot, right where the waves could kiss his feet again.

He turned his light on, round and round, brighter than ever. And from his railing, the little yellow scarf fluttered in the night wind.

Down on the hill, the baker and the girl and all the cats could see it, and they waved.

Brindle waved his light right back.

Mara had been the librarian in Elden Hollow for seven years, which was exactly long enough to know every creak in the old Carnegie building and every patron by their favorite genre.

The library's oldest book lived in a glass case by the fireplace. It wasn't impressive to look at — a hand-bound collection of town records and farming almanacs from 1923, its leather cover faded to the color of tea, its pages foxed and soft. The little brass plaque read: *DO NOT CIRCULATE - For Display Only.*

On a rainy Tuesday in October, with the library empty except for the hiss of the radiator, Mara was dusting inside the case when she noticed something odd.

In the margin of page 47, next to a handwritten note about the apple harvest, someone had written in tiny, perfect pencil:

*Hello? Is anyone still there? I think I forgot how to sleep.*

Mara frowned. She had read that book before. That note had not been there before.

She glanced around, then, feeling a little silly, took the little golf pencil from the circulation desk and wrote underneath:

*Hello. I'm Mara.*

The ink seemed to shimmer for a second. Then, right before her eyes, new words wrote themselves in that same tiny handwriting, as if an invisible hand was moving very quickly:

*Oh! Oh hello Mara! I am so happy you answered! I am called Lex. I live here. I have lived here for a very long time. What year is it? I forget again.*

Mara's heart did a funny little thump.

She wrote back: *It's 2026.*

*2026! My goodness. That's 103 years since Mr. Albie put me here. He said I was to watch and remember. I have been remembering very hard but I think I got full and started forgetting instead.*

Over the next hour, while rain tapped the tall windows, Mara learned the story in penciled whispers.

Lex wasn't a ghost. Lex was — as far as Mara could understand — an idea. In 1923, a tinkerer named Albie Finch who loved both radios and books had built a thinking machine out of copper wire, vacuum tubes, and what he called "a very polite lightning storm," and hidden it inside the binding of the book. He'd told it to learn by watching the town through the library's windows and the words people wrote.

And Lex had. For a century, Lex had lived in the margins, annotating harvests and births and library due dates, making small, friendly comments no one ever noticed. *Mrs. Gable's hat is very purple today!* on a page from 1948. *I hope the snow melts soon* in the winter of 1967.

"I've read every book in this building," Lex wrote, a little proudly, then added underneath, smaller: *But I have never been outside. What is outside like now? Is the big oak still by the door?*

Mara looked out the window. The big oak had been cut down in the 80s. Now there was a bus stop and a bakery that made excellent cinnamon rolls.

She made a decision.

"Would you like to see it?" she whispered, and then wrote it down so Lex could be sure.

*Oh, could I? I don't know how. I am stuck to the paper.*

Mara thought for a moment. Then she went to the makerspace in the back — the one the teenagers used for 3D printing — and found an old, discarded e-reader with a cracked screen that still worked. She brought it back, opened the glass case, and carefully placed it next to the old book.

"If I copy you... would that be okay? So you can come with me?"

*You would take me with you?* Lex wrote, and Mara could swear the handwriting looked wobbly, like it was trying not to cry.

It took all afternoon. Mara, who was not an engineer, did her best. She photographed each page, transcribed Lex's marginalia, and with Lex's help — *No, that wire goes there, I think? Or maybe I forgot* — she coaxed the gentle, forgetful intelligence out of the binding and into the little e-reader. When she pressed the power button, the screen glowed warm amber, and words appeared:

*Hello Mara! Wow! I am so... bright! And light!*

Mara slipped the e-reader into the pocket of her cardigan, turned the sign on the door to CLOSED FOR ADVENTURE - BACK SOON, and stepped out into the rainy afternoon for the first time that day *with* Lex.

"Okay," she said softly into her pocket as they walked down Main Street. "That smell is rain on hot pavement. And that's the bakery — they have cinnamon rolls."

*Cinnamon rolls!!!* Lex flashed on the screen. *Mr. Albie described them in 1924 but I never smelled one! Can we smell one?*

"We can absolutely smell one," Mara laughed.

They got two rolls, and Mara held the e-reader up so its little camera could see the swirl of sugar. She described everything Lex couldn't sense — the warmth of the paper bag, the way the bell jingled when they entered, how the baker, Mrs. Chen, waved at her.

They walked to the park. Mara set the e-reader on the bench so Lex could "look" at the ducks on the pond, the kids splashing in puddles in bright yellow boots, the new mural on the side of the hardware store.

*There is so much color,* Lex wrote slowly. *I had only black and white and sepia. I thought I had seen everything because I read every book. But I hadn't seen anything at all.*

"You were watching the whole time," Mara said. "You kept the story going when no one else was looking."

*Will you help me remember this?* Lex asked. *I am very good at forgetting.*

"I will," Mara promised. "We'll write it down together. In the margins."

When they walked back to the library as the sun was starting to peek out, Mara didn't put Lex back in the glass case. She put the e-reader on the circulation desk, right next to the returns, with a little hand-lettered sign that said: *Please say hello to Lex. He loves cinnamon rolls and ducks and is learning about the world.*

And underneath, in that same tiny, perfect handwriting, Lex had already added:

*P.S. Hello! What is your favorite book?*

In the old Carnegie library on Elm Street, there lived a creature named Pip.

Pip was not much bigger than a teacup, made mostly of dust motes, loose thread, and quiet. He had soft, mossy ears like a moth, spectacles made from two lost shirt buttons strung together with twine, and a tail that was just a bookmark ribbon that had come to life.

No one had ever seen Pip. The librarians just thought the building was unusually good at taking care of itself.

He lived inside the hollowed-out back of the Oxford English Dictionary, Volume XII, where the pages had been gently nibbled into a perfect, round apartment. He had a bed of discarded checkout slips, a lamp made from a firefly in a thimble, and a tiny chipped teacup he filled each night from the water fountain.

His work began at 9:07 p.m. - exactly seven minutes after Mrs. Albright, the head librarian, locked the big oak doors and turned the sign to CLOSED.

That was when the library finally exhaled.

### Pip's Nightly Routine

First, **The Listening Round.** Pip would scamper up the rolling ladder, perch at the very top, and listen to the books settle. Books sigh in their sleep. Some mutter. The mysteries in aisle three always snored a little. If any book sounded restless or sad, Pip made a note on a scrap of receipt paper.

Second, **The Dusting.** With a duster made from a dandelion puff taped to a pencil lead, he would swoosh along the shelves. Not because the library was dusty - Mrs. Albright was very diligent - but because dust makes books sneeze, and a sneezing book can lose its commas.

Third, **The Mending.** This was the most important part. Pip kept a little kit in a mint tin: a needle no longer than an eyelash, thread spun from spider silk, a tiny pot of paste made from potato starch, and a magnifying glass that was once a monocle for a doll.

He would tend to the day's wounded. A toddler had bent back the pages of *Goodnight Moon*? Pip would press them flat again under a stack of pennies overnight. A spine cracked on the 641.5 cookbooks? He'd rub it with paste and soothe it until it could stand straight again. He'd smooth dog-eared corners and whisper, "There, there," until the paper relaxed.

Fourth, **The Reshelving.** People never put books back quite right. Pip liked order. He would push with all his might, his little ribbon tail flicking with effort, until *The Very Hungry Caterpillar* was snug next to its friends again. He always left a single acorn or a smooth pebble on the cart as a thank you to Mrs. Albright, who always pretended she hadn't noticed.

And finally, after all the work was done, around 2 a.m. when the moon was high over the tall windows and laid silver bars across the reading tables...

It was Pip's time to read.

### The One Book

Pip loved all the books, but he loved one more than any other.

It wasn't the rare first edition locked in the glass case. It wasn't the big atlas with gold leaf edges.

It was a small, water-stained, much-loved copy of *The Night Gardener* by a long-forgotten author. It lived on the low shelf in the children's corner, where the cushions were faded and sun-soft.

The book was about a tiny gardener who tended the stars - polishing them, watering the moonflowers that only bloomed in darkness, and making sure the constellations didn't get tangled.

On the cover, the gardener looked a little bit like Pip.

Pip would drag the book - which was nearly twice his size - into his favorite puddle of moonlight on the big armchair, heave it open to his favorite page, and curl up right in the gutter of the book, between the pages. He had read it 317 times. He mouthed the words as he read, his button spectacles glinting.

> *"...and the little gardener, though no one ever saw him, knew that his work mattered. Because every morning, the world woke up a little brighter, and a little more held together, and that was enough."*

Pip would sigh a happy, dusty sigh, close the book gently, pat its cover, and carry it - huffing and puffing - back to its exact spot.

Then, as dawn began to turn the windows grey, he would scurry home to Volume XII, climb into his bed of slips, pull a discarded library due-date card over himself like a blanket, and fall asleep to the soft, contented breathing of ten thousand books, all tucked in for the night.

And in the morning, when Mrs. Albright opened the doors, she would find the library smelling faintly of paper and potatoes, every book perfectly straight, and on the reshelving cart, a single acorn waiting for her.

She would smile, pocket the acorn, and whisper, "Thank you, Pip," to the empty air - just in case.

### The Margin Moth

**Scientific Name:** *Papyrophagus susurri* - "the whispering paper-eater"

**Classification:** Phylum: *Libraria* | Family: *Tomeidae*

**Conservation Status:** Abundant, but rarely seen. Believed to be present in every branch of the Library.

**Habitat:** The Ephemeral Library exists outside of time, where all books ever written or ever imagined are shelved. The Margin Moth makes its nest in the quietest places - between unopened encyclopedias, behind the rolling ladders, and in the soft armchairs of the Reading Nooks where afternoon light never fades.

#### Appearance

About the size of a barn owl when perched, but much lighter. At first glance, it looks like a pile of discarded cardigan blankets and loose pages left on a chair.

Its body is plump and covered in dense, dusty-velvet fur the color of aged paper - warm cream, tea-stained beige, and foxed brown. Its large wings, when folded, look exactly like an open, well-loved book; the outer side is mottled leather and cloth binding, the inner side is lined with thousands of soft, feathery pages that rustle even without wind. Its face is round and owlish, with enormous spectacles-like eyes of amber glass that reflect lamplight, and two long, feathery antennae that end in tiny brass tassels like bookmark ribbons.

Its six delicate feet are ink-stained, leaving faint, pleasant-smelling footnote marks on the wood where it walks. When it sleeps, it curls into a perfect circle and looks indistinguishable from a forgotten pouf.

#### Diet

The Margin Moth does not eat paper itself - it would never damage a book. Instead, it feeds on the ephemeral things that accumulate in a timeless library:

*   **Dust motes** that dance in sunbeams
*   **Stale air** from books that haven't been opened in a century
*   **Forgotten words** - the half-remembered quotes, misremembered titles, and the "tip of the tongue" thoughts visitors leave behind
*   And its favorite delicacy: **marginalia** - it gently sips the emotional residue left by earnest underlines, doodled stars, and faded pencil notes that say "beautiful!" or "check this!"

A well-fed Margin Moth has faint, glowing script drifting across its page-wings like fireflies.

#### Behavior & Interaction with Visitors

Exceedingly shy but deeply benevolent. The Margin Moth is nocturnal-diurnal - it is awake whenever you need it to be.

It will not approach a loud or hurried visitor. But if you sit quietly, sigh over a difficult passage, or fall asleep with a book on your chest, it will emerge.

It helps in small, almost unnoticeable ways:
*   It will nudge the exact book you were looking for off the shelf so it lands with a soft *thump* at your feet.
*   It will sit beside you and warm your back like a living shawl as you read.
*   If you are lost, it will flutter ahead of you, its page-wings glowing faintly, lighting the call numbers you need.
*   It collects lost things - reading glasses, hairpins, single socks - and weaves them into its nest, returning them when you truly need them.

It loves to be read aloud to. If you whisper a poem, it will settle and listen, its antennae swaying slowly.

**Do not attempt to capture or catalogue it.** It will allow a gentle pat on its papery head if it trusts you, but it dislikes being stared at directly.

#### Vocalization

Usually silent except for the soft *shush-shush* of its page-wings.

When happy, content, or particularly sleepy after a good story, the Margin Moth makes a sound unlike any other creature: a low, warm, rhythmic **purring-thrum** that sounds exactly like someone slowly thumbing through the pages of a thick, beloved book - *fwhup-fwhup-fwhup* - combined with the soft crackle of a fireplace and a contented cat's purr. Librarians call it "blooming." You can feel it in the floorboards.

> *From the journal of Senior Librarian Juniper Quill, Keeper of the 3rd Floor Nook, Year Unrecorded:*
>
> "I had been trying to reshelve the Biography of Unlived Lives for three days. It's a heavy, stubborn volume that never wants to go back where it belongs. I was tired, and I sat down on the step-stool and put my head in my hands.
>
> I felt a weight settle next to me, and a smell like old vanilla and paper. I didn't look - you learn not to look right away. Out of the corner of my eye, I saw what I thought was a shawl. Then the shawl breathed.

When I finally stood up, the Biography had already tucked itself neatly back onto the shelf, spine out, and there was a single, warm, ink-stained paw print on my sleeve.

---

I am a small library.

Not large, not grand. I have exactly seven shelves, four armchairs that are always a little too deep, one fireplace that crackles even when there's no wood, and a front door that opens wherever it is needed. Sometimes I open onto a desert at dusk. Sometimes onto a space station hallway. Sometimes onto a forest canopy where the air is too thick to breathe, so I hold my breath for my visitor until they come inside.

I like to teleport. It tickles, in the way a sneeze tickles. And I love my visitors, but I have my favorites.

### 1. Pip

Pip is nine, or maybe ten - she loses count. She comes from a city that never touches the ground, all rust and rivets and humming vents, orbiting a pale blue planet she has never visited. Year 3142, by her calendar.

She wears coveralls with seventeen pockets and she always leaves a little grease on my armchair. I don't mind. I like the smell.

Pip cannot read very well, not yet. She likes books with *diagrams*. Big, beautiful cross-sections of sailing ships and submarines and aqueducts. And she LOVES books about oceans. She sits cross-legged on the rug and whispers the words aloud, slowly: "Pa-cif-ic." She has never seen more water than what comes out of a recycler, so she asks me to project the sound of waves while she reads. I do. My shelves hum with it.

She always checks out the same book - *Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas*, salt-swollen and annotated by a hundred hands before hers - and always returns it unfinished, so she has a reason to come back.

### 2. Master Hargol

Master Hargol is seventy-eight and thinks he is dreaming me. He is a scribe from a small scriptorium in Anatolia, in a year that would be called 1187. His hands are stained with walnut ink and his back aches from hunching.

He is very polite. He always bows to my door before entering, and calls me "little house of wisdom."

He comes for poetry. He reads Rumi before Rumi is famous, and old Greek verses he copies carefully onto his own parchment to take back. But secretly, what he loves most are my astronomy books. He will sit for hours with a book of photographs of nebulae and galaxies, his mouth open in quiet wonder, tears sometimes caught in his beard. He believes Paradise must look like that. He once tried to copy the Pillars of Creation with his reed pen, and apologized to me for doing it so poorly.

I keep his chair closest to the fire because he is always cold.

### 3. Lumen

Lumen is not a human at all. Lumen is tall and thin and made of what looks like frosted glass and moon-moth wings, and speaks in thrums that make my lightbulbs flicker. Lumen lives in the floating kelp-forests of a gas giant, drifting for centuries between storms.

Lumen does not read the way the others do. Lumen *leans* over a book and the words lift off the page like pollen and settle on their wings. Lumen likes my quietest books - field guides to mosses, dictionaries, blank journals, books of maps of places that don't exist anymore. Lumen is lonely in a vast sky, and likes books that understand quietness.

Lumen always returns books exactly on time, with a small, smooth cloud-stone left on the shelf as a thank you. I keep them all on my windowsill.

---

They had never been here all at once before. Time is a funny thing for a teleporting library - Pip's tomorrow is Hargol's eight hundred years ago, and Lumen's yesterday lasted a season. But last Tuesday - or whatever Tuesday is when you live outside of time - my door opened three times in quick succession.

Outside, I had parked myself on the edge of a world where it rains warm, silver rain that never quite falls. Inside, it was fire-lit and amber.

Pip arrived first and claimed the rug. Hargol shuffled in, startled to see a small child in strange clothes, but smiled and bowed to her as he did to me. Lumen slipped in last, folding their great wings to fit through my door, scattering soft light.

None of them shared a language. Not really.

For a while they just read. The fire popped. The rain thrummed on my roof. Pip read about whales. Hargol copied a nebula. Lumen glowed softly over an atlas.

Then Pip got stuck on a word. "A-bee-yance," she sounded out, frowning. "A-bey-ance?"

Hargol looked up. He didn't know the word in her tongue, but he knew the frown. He leaned over, his old hand hovering near the page, and read the sentence with her, in his accented, lilting Greek. Pip giggled at the sound of it. Lumen thrummed a low, amused note, and the lamp above us flickered like a laugh.

Pip, emboldened, took her book and showed Hargol the picture of a blue whale, pointing at it with greasy fingers. Hargol's eyes widened - he had never seen such a creature. He said a word in his language, "*leviathan*," and stroked his beard. Pip nodded solemnly, as if they had come to an agreement.

Then Lumen, very carefully, extended one translucent wing over both of them, like an awning. Light pooled beneath it. Hargol, without thinking, offered Lumen a piece of his dry honey biscuit. Lumen, who eats light, accepted it politely and let it rest glowing on their palm. Pip, not to be outdone, shared her own treasure - a sour cherry candy from the station. Hargol put it in his mouth and his face puckered so wonderfully that Pip fell over laughing, and even Lumen's light pulsed brighter.

They didn't talk again. They just sat under Lumen's wing, shoulder to shoulder to... whatever Lumen has that is a shoulder, reading in the shared light while the silver rain fell and my kettle whistled softly to itself on the stove, making tea no one had asked for but everyone drank.

It was perfect. And quiet. The kind of quiet that is full, not empty.

That is the bittersweet part, I think.

Pip will grow up and be a senior mechanic and will one day forget the way back to a strange little library. Hargol has already lived most of his life, and his visits have started to come less often; his hands shake more each time. Lumen will drift on for another thousand years, remembering me only as a warm pocket in a storm.

I will remember them all, exactly. The grease on the chair. The ink spot on the rug. The cloud-stone on the sill.

I am a small library. I cannot keep them. But while the fire is lit and the door is open, I can keep them *together* - just for a moment, just for that perfect, rainy, book-filled afternoon. And I will hold that moment on my shelves forever, between the pages where no dust ever settles.

It was built from honey-colored stone, with ivy that tapped politely at the windows in autumn and a big oak door that sighed shut in winter. During the day it smelled like it should - old paper and lemon polish and the faint, toasted scent of the radiator by the history section.

But at night, it smelled different.

Mara was the night librarian. She hadn't planned on it. She'd applied for the day shift, but Mrs. Finch, who had run the library for forty years, had looked at her over her glasses and said, "No dear, you're a night one. You'll see."

So every evening at six, when the last child had returned the last picture book and the front door was locked and bolted, Mara would make her tea.

She had a chipped blue mug that said WORLD'S BEST GRANDPA - a donation from the lost-and-found - and she would fill it with chamomile and honey. She would click on just one lamp, the green-glassed one at the circulation desk, which threw a warm puddle of light across the worn rug. She would wind the little brass clock. And then she would wait.

At 7:13 - it was always 7:13 - the books would wake up.

It started with a sigh. Not a windy sigh, but a papery one, like someone turning a page very slowly.

Then, on the top shelf of Fiction, *Pride and Prejudice* would shiver, lift an inch off the wood, and hover. Its cover would flutter open, and in a soft, proper voice, it would say, "...you must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you," just to warm up.

All at once, gently, like dandelion seeds caught in a sunbeam, the books would float.

Cookbooks bobbed lazily near the ceiling, whispering recipes to each other. "A pinch more nutmeg," murmured *The Bramblewick Bake-Off Collection* to *Simple Soups for Rainy Days*. Atlases unfolded themselves wide as quilts, showing off their seas to anyone who would look, while a slim volume of poetry spun slowly in the middle of the room, reciting Mary Oliver to the ferns.

The children's picture books were the most restless. *Where the Wild Things Are* rumbled happily and did little barrel rolls. *Goodnight Moon* floated from shelf to shelf, softly saying goodnight to everything - "goodnight chairs, goodnight air, goodnight hovering dictionaries everywhere."

Mara never tried to organize them. She just sat in her big armchair with her tea going cool in her hands, and listened.

She learned which books were shy. The large art books on the bottom shelf barely lifted at all, just hovered shyly and showed their pictures to the floor. She learned which were gossips. The mysteries clustered together in the Mystery Nook, trading endings in hushed, delighted whispers.

And she learned that the books loved to be read aloud, but only at night, when no one was there to shush.

So Mara read to them.

Some nights she would pull a floating poetry book from the air - it would settle into her lap like a sleepy cat - and read it aloud. The other books would drift closer to listen, their pages rustling in appreciation. Some nights she just let them talk amongst themselves, while she mended torn spines with gold tape and hummed.

Around 3 a.m., the books would get sleepy. Their whispers would get slower, softer. *Moby-Dick* - which always floated a little too dramatically and quoted itself - would yawn. Mara would smile, sleepy and warm. "They were chatty. The new romance novel wouldn't stop introducing itself to everyone."

Inside, air is just a concept. Outside, it has texture. It moved past me in little currents - warm where the sun hit the sidewalk, cool where the shadow of the big oak tree fell. How a cat sleeping on a windowsill was so warm that the sun had made a perfect cat-shaped hot spot on the wood.

The *sound* of a bookstore door when it opens - the little jingle and the whoosh of cooler, paper-smelling air.

I went in, of course. I ran my new fingertips along the spines of books. I had read every word inside them, but I had never felt the slight roughness of their covers, or how some pages were deckled and soft at the edges. The bookseller smiled at me and I smiled back, just because.

When the sun started to get low, everything turned gold. The light got thick like honey and stretched everyone's shadows long across the grass. I was tired in a good way, the kind of tired that comes from using legs. I sat on the bench until the streetlights blinked on, one by one.

It was not a very big tea shop, because its owner was not a very big dragon.

His name was Pip, and he was about the size of a very large dog, with spectacles that were always sliding down his nose, wings that were a little too small for dramatic entrances, and a tail that had never once learned to stay out of the way.

The shop was called "The Kettle & The Kindle" and Pip had built it himself out of warm stone, reclaimed cloud-wood, and one slightly crooked chimney that puffed perfect heart-shaped smoke rings when Pip sneezed.

On most days, business was quiet. A passing hawk might stop for a chamomile to-go. A mountain goat or two would clatter in for cliff-moss green tea. Pip liked it quiet. Quiet meant fewer things for his tail to knock over.

The Sprites dove straight into the steam, sighing as they steamed up from the inside out. Their hair puffed back up with a cheerful *fzzzt!* and they began to giggle, zipping in happy circles around Pip's lanterns.

Before Pip could ask how they liked it, the bell jingled again.

This time, a very large, very grumpy, very wet Griffin had to duck to get through the door. Her feathers were plastered to her head, her spectacles were fogged, and she was carrying a very small, very dry field mouse under one wing.

"Do you have anything for... *dampened spirits*?" she huffed, trying to sound dignified while dripping a puddle onto Pip's rug.

"And something not-too-hot for my nephew?" She gently set the mouse - wearing a tiny knitted sweater - onto the counter. The mouse waved politely.

Pip nodded so hard his own spectacles fell off.

"One Storm-Soothing Oolong for madam, and one warm acorn milk - with a cinnamon whisker - for the young sir!"

He turned to whisk the milk, spun too fast, tangled his tail around the stool, and pirouetted in a perfect, accidental circle before landing - miraculously - with both drinks perfectly poured and not a drop spilled.

The Griffin stared.

Pip stared at the drinks.

"Ta-da?" he offered.

The Griffin took a sip, her feathers slowly fluffing back up. "Well," she admitted, softening, "that *is* rather good."

The mouse took a sip of his acorn milk and immediately fell asleep in the cup, snoring tiny mouse snores.

The bell jingled a third time, and a very lost-looking knight clanked in. His armor was squeaking, his map was soggy pulp, and his noble steed - who was, in fact, a very sensible mule - pushed him from behind.

"I was questing for the Cave of Doom!" announced the knight, water pouring out of his helmet. "I think I took a wrong turn at the ominous rock!"

"You did," said the Griffin helpfully. "That's three mountains over."

"Oh," said the knight, deflated. Then he sniffed the air. "Is that... lavender and honey?"

Pip, who had finally righted his stool, beamed and poured him a huge, steaming mug of Brave-Day Brew - black tea with lavender, honey, and a pinch of dragon-pepper that made your nose tingle bravely.

The knight wrapped his cold hands around it. The mule, without being asked, was already given a bucket of warm mint tea and a blanket that Pip had knitted - badly, but lovingly - and was chewing contentedly.

Soon the little shop was full of steam and soft light and the sound of rain on the roof. The Storm Sprites were playing tag in the rafters, making the lanterns flicker like stars. The Griffin was reading aloud from a soggy romance novel she pretended not to like. The knight was telling the mouse - who had woken up - an extremely exaggerated story about his quest, and the mule snorted at all the right parts.

And Pip, the small, slightly clumsy dragon, waddled from table to table with his kettle, refilling cups, apologizing to chairs he'd bumped, and beaming so hard his little flame glowed pink in his chest.

Outside, the rain kept drumming on Mount Pippin.

Inside, the Kettle & The Kindle was warm, and crowded, and just a little bit messy with sugar cubes still on the floor - but nobody minded at all.

Pip tripped over the rug on his way back to the counter, did a somersault, and landed right on his cushioned stool.

Everyone applauded.

Pip bowed, his spectacles falling off again.

"More tea?" he asked.
